content: Giardia lamblia, also known as Lamblia intestinalis or Giardia duodenalis, is a flagellated protozoan parasite that causes the disease giardiasis. It belongs to the Eukaryota domain and is classified under the Diplomonadida group, within the family Hexamitidae, subfamily Giardiinae, and genus Giardia. Giardia lamblia infects both humans and a variety of animals, including cats, dogs, cows, beavers, deer, and sheep. It is a microaerophilic organism, meaning it thrives in environments with low oxygen levels. The trophozoite form of Giardia lamblia is pear-shaped and has a distinctive morphology, characterized by two identical nuclei, a ventral adhesive disc that allows it to attach to the intestinal lining of the host, and multiple flagella for motility. The genome of Giardia lamblia consists of approximately 1.2 million base pairs with an average GC content of 46%. Its genetic material is organized into five linear chromosomes, each flanked by telomere sequences (5’TAGGG3’), similar to other eukaryotic organisms. The life cycle of Giardia lamblia begins with the excretion of non-infective cysts in the feces of an infected host. Once in the environment, these cysts become infective. The cysts are characterized by their four nuclei and retracted cytoplasm. When ingested by a new host, the cysts transform into trophozoites, which are the active, feeding, and motile form of the parasite. Trophozoites replicate asexually through longitudinal binary fission. Both trophozoites and cysts are excreted in the feces, but only the cysts are capable of surviving outside the host. Trophozoites are distinguished by their large karyosomes and the absence of peripheral chromatin, which gives their nuclei a halo-like appearance. Scanning electron microscopy (SEM) has provided detailed images of Giardia lamblia at various stages of its life cycle. These include: The dorsal surface of a Giardia protozoan isolated from a rat’s intestine. The mucosal surface of the small intestine of a gerbil infested with Giardia species. A Giardia lamblia protozoan in a late stage of cell division, forming a heart-shaped structure as it prepares to divide into two organisms. The ventral surface of a Giardia muris trophozoite. The ultrastructural details of an oblong-shaped Giardia cyst. A Giardia muris trophozoite adhering to the mucosal surface of a rat’s intestine. A Giardia lamblia protozoan caught in the process of cell division. A Giardia muris protozoan attaching itself to the microvillous border of an intestinal epithelial cell. Giardia lamblia parasites visualized using an indirect immunofluorescence test for giardiasis. In terms of differential diagnosis, Giardia lamblia infection must be distinguished from other causes of viral, bacterial, and parasitic gastroenteritis. Small bowel diarrhea caused by Giardia is typically watery and voluminous, with fewer than 5 white blood cells (WBCs) per high-power field. In contrast, large bowel diarrhea is often mucousy or bloody, with less volume and more than 10 WBCs per high-power field. The severity of symptoms can vary depending on the patient’s immune status, with some cases presenting with WBC counts as high as 1000.
